report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

We examined 56 columns across 16 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 16 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

#### File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. **8 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Files not run on their own
2 files could not be read, so they were not run and need to be checked again: this may be a problem of the computer that ran the check, not of the files.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 9 scripts: 2 ran without error, 2 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 3 were run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **1 script uses an object or function that only another script defines**, so in the second run that script was loaded first, in the same session: `YF_Model_Stage1_Convergence.R` after `YF_Model_LHS.R`. Such a script should `source()` the other itself, since it does not run on its own.

text.text: 233 References: 28 outbreaks, but specific impacts are unknown.
This modeling analysis estimates the individual 27 and combined effects of vaccination coverage and response timing on recent yellow fever 28 outbreaks in Africa.
Yellow fever (YF) is a vaccine-preventable disease caused by YF virus, which is transmitted by mosquitoes in Africa and South America.
In 2016 a yellow fever (YF) epidemic in Africa depleted the global supply of YF vaccines [1].
text.formatted: In 2016 a yellow fever (YF) epidemic in Africa depleted the global supply of YF vaccines <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: This led to the creation of the Eliminate Yellow Fever Epidemics (EYE) strategy by the World Health Organization (WHO) and Gavi [2].
text.formatted: This led to the creation of the Eliminate Yellow Fever Epidemics (EYE) strategy by the World Health Organization (WHO) and Gavi <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: The goal of the EYE strategy has been to eliminate YF epidemics by 2026 through increased investment and support in YF vaccination and laboratory diagnostic capacity [2].
text.formatted: The goal of the EYE strategy has been to eliminate YF epidemics by 2026 through increased investment and support in YF vaccination and laboratory diagnostic capacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: It is estimated that over 336 million individuals have been vaccinated in Africa since the EYE strategy [3].
text.formatted: It is estimated that over 336 million individuals have been vaccinated in Africa since the EYE strategy <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: Despite this effort, there have continued to be recent YF outbreaks in multiple African and South American countries [3, 4].
text.formatted: Despite this effort, there have continued to be recent YF outbreaks in multiple African and South American countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4]</ref>.

text.text: In 2024, 15 countries in Africa reported YF cases to the WHO, requiring vaccination interventions [3].
text.formatted: In 2024, 15 countries in Africa reported YF cases to the WHO, requiring vaccination interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: As the EYE strategy transitions to greater country-level ownership after 2026 [5], it is critical to assess its impact, as well as how both the coverage and timing of YF vaccination affect the trajectory of outbreaks.
text.formatted: As the EYE strategy transitions to greater country-level ownership after 2026 <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>, it is critical to assess its impact, as well as how both the coverage and timing of YF vaccination affect the trajectory of outbreaks.

text.text: A focus of the EYE strategy has been on increasing YF vaccination coverage and availability.
There are three main YF vaccination strategies: routine childhood vaccination, preventative mass vaccination campaigns (PMVCs), and reactive vaccination campaigns.
In YFendemic countries, routine childhood vaccination for YF occurs usually at 9 months of age.
Preventative mass vaccination campaigns are designed to increase YF vaccination coverage in endemic areas.

Timely reactive vaccination during outbreaks has been a major component of the EYE strategy, emphasizing immediate YF vaccination using vaccines already available incountry followed by larger mass vaccination campaigns [2, 6, 7].
text.formatted: Timely reactive vaccination during outbreaks has been a major component of the EYE strategy, emphasizing immediate YF vaccination using vaccines already available incountry followed by larger mass vaccination campaigns <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7]</ref>.

text.text: The International Coordinating Group of Vaccine Provision (ICG) manages the global YF vaccine stockpile [2].
text.formatted: The International Coordinating Group of Vaccine Provision (ICG) manages the global YF vaccine stockpile <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: Because the YF vaccine takes roughly a year to produce, the ICG stockpile is designed to ensure that sufficient doses are available at all times [2].
text.formatted: Because the YF vaccine takes roughly a year to produce, the ICG stockpile is designed to ensure that sufficient doses are available at all times <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: When a YF outbreak occurs, countries are recommended to promptly apply for YF vaccines.
The WHO advises that there should be a maximum 10-day period between submission of the vaccine request and arrival [6].
text.formatted: The WHO advises that there should be a maximum 10-day period between submission of the vaccine request and arrival <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: Countries should then implement the reactive YF vaccination campaign within 10 days after receiving the vaccines [6].
text.formatted: Countries should then implement the reactive YF vaccination campaign within 10 days after receiving the vaccines <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: Thus, a 20-day window is the approximate guideline for the time between YF outbreak detection and initiation of reactive mass vaccination.
The EYE strategy recommends a YF immunization coverage of "greater than 80%, with a 60-80% security threshold," to prevent epidemics [2].
text.formatted: The EYE strategy recommends a YF immunization coverage of "greater than 80%, with a 60-80% security threshold," to prevent epidemics <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, the EYE strategy aimed to achieve at least 50% vaccination coverage in high-risk African countries via PMVCs [2].
text.formatted: Additionally, the EYE strategy aimed to achieve at least 50% vaccination coverage in high-risk African countries via PMVCs <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: There is a need to understand how these thresholds influence YF outbreaks in local contexts, as well as how vaccination timing and coverage synergistically influence YF outbreaks.
Given these questions and the upcoming transition of the EYE strategy, our study had three main goals.
First, we developed mathematical models to assess the effects of immunization coverage and reactive vaccination timing on YF outbreaks.
Second, we fit these models to recent outbreaks in Ghana (2021-2022) and South Sudan (2023-2024).
Lastly, we simulated the effects of different YF immunization coverage and timing scenarios on projected outbreak size and mortality.

To model the effects of varying vaccination timing and coverage on YF outbreaks in African countries, we developed deterministic transmission models that incorporate stochastic surveillance reporting.
The human (h) population was simulated using a Susceptible-Exposed-Infectious-Recovered (SEIR) framework, coupled with a Susceptible-Exposed-Infectious (SEI) model for the mosquito (v) population.
This model framework was chosen because YF is an acute immunizing infection transmitted via mosquitoes, and it is assumed that infection and/or vaccination in humans provides lifelong immunity.
For the purposes of analyzing outbreak scenarios and outcomes, we assumed that these were closed outbreaks (excluding human births, non-YF related deaths, and migration during the outbreaks).
The underlying compartmental model framework is shown in Figure 1.
text.formatted: The underlying compartmental model framework is shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: The human compartments include susceptible (Sh), exposed (Eh), symptomatic/severe infected (Ih), asymptomatic/non-severe infected (Ah), toxic (Th), and recovered (Rh).
The mosquito compartments include susceptible (Sv), exposed (Ev) and infected (Iv).
The full model, parameter notation, and equations are included in the Appendix (Figure S1).
text.formatted: The full model, parameter notation, and equations are included in the Appendix (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: The compartments for the SEIR-SEI yellow fever (YF) model framework are shown in blue for humans and orange for mosquitoes.
Susceptible mosquitoes are exposed by biting an infected human with asymptomatic or severe infection.
These exposed mosquitoes go on to develop active infection and then can transmit to susceptible humans.
There are three pathways for susceptible humans upon exposure to YF virus from an infected mosquito: 1.
Those who are vaccinated prior to infection join the recovered compartment.
Those who are exposed and are asymptomatic/non-severe recover.
Those who are exposed and become severely infected and go on to the toxic state to either recover or die.

The model framework reflects separate pathways for humans who are exposed (Eh) to YF virus based on the force of infection (a function of the biting rate (a), transmission probability from vector to host (b), and ratio of infectious mosquitoes per human).
Exposed individuals become infectious at an incubation rate (σh), and a proportion (δ) become severe infected individuals (Ih), while the remaining are asymptomatic/non-severe cases (Ah).
The severe cases transition to the toxic state (Th) and then either die (Dh) or recover (Rh).
We included a transition rate (η) between infected to toxic, which differs from the rate to recovery [8].
text.formatted: We included a transition rate (η) between infected to toxic, which differs from the rate to recovery <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: The asymptomatic/non-severe cases recover at rate γh.

These separate pathways reflect the fact that YF surveillance systems in African countries rely on passive reporting and detect primarily severe/symptomatic cases [9]; a similar framework was used to model the 2016 Angola YF outbreak [10].
text.formatted: These separate pathways reflect the fact that YF surveillance systems in African countries rely on passive reporting and detect primarily severe/symptomatic cases <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>; a similar framework was used to model the 2016 Angola YF outbreak <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: Model calibration and projections were fitted to the number of severe/symptomatic cases (Ih), as this compartment most closely reflects the observed surveillance data.
Hereafter, the term "cases" refers to these severe/symptomatic individuals.
We used a partially observed Markov process (POMP) modeling framework [11], given that infected cases are only partially captured by the surveillance data.
text.formatted: We used a partially observed Markov process (POMP) modeling framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>, given that infected cases are only partially captured by the surveillance data.

text.text: Because our goal was to create a model framework that could be flexible enough to use in different outbreak settings, we intentionally adopted a simplified, transparent modeling framework requiring estimation of a minimum number of parameters.
We made an a priori assumption that outbreaks began with a single infected human (Ih = 1).
Given that YF cases are likely to be under-ascertained in many African countries, we estimated the reporting ratio (ρ), defined as (ascertained cases)/(total cases).
Additionally, we estimated the mosquito-to-human ratio (m) and the initial number of infected mosquitoes (Iv) as independent parameters in the model.

The total mosquito population (Nv) was modeled as being at steady-state for the outbreak period, but a temperature-dependent mortality rate (μ v ) balanced by an equivalent recruitment rate was used to simulate vector turnover (Appendix).
The values for the fixed and estimated parameters in the models are shown in Table 1.
text.formatted: The values for the fixed and estimated parameters in the models are shown in Table <ref type="table">1</ref>.

text.text: Since Aedes aegypti is the mosquito species responsible for YF epidemics in Africa [12], we used Aedes aegypti-specific parameters.
text.formatted: Since Aedes aegypti is the mosquito species responsible for YF epidemics in Africa <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>, we used Aedes aegypti-specific parameters.

text.text: We captured seasonal dynamics by using temperaturedependent functions for biting rate (a), mortality rate (μ v ), and vector incubation rate (σ v ), based on functions and mean parameter estimates for Aedes aegypti and YF (Appendix, Table S1) [13] [14] [15].

text.text: We calibrated the reporting ratio (ρ), number of initial infected mosquitoes (Iv), and the mosquito-to-human ratio (m) for the Ghana and South Sudan outbreaks by fitting modelestimated cases to observed daily YF cases, assuming estimated vaccination coverage and reactive vaccination timing for each outbreak as described above.
We calibrated the size of the Ih compartment to the number of observed cases on a daily basis, using data on symptom onset from both outbreaks.
We implemented our model using the pomp package in R [11].

text.text: We used likelihood-based parameter estimation and sampled the parameter space using Latin Hypercube Sampling (LHS) with 10,000 iterations.

The model was calibrated by minimizing the negative log-likelihood (NLL), assuming the observed cases for each outbreak day followed independent Poisson distributions (evaluated using the dmeasure function).
To account for uncertainty, we first selected all parameter sets within 10 NLL units of the best 206 fitting parameter set (Figure S4-S5).

text.text: To perform the scenario analyses of different vaccination 207 coverages and response times, we took likelihood-weighted samples of these parameter sets 208 (4,400 per outbreak) and used the outputs from those likelihood-weighted samples to estimate 209 the size of outbreaks under different scenarios (Appendix).

Likelihood weights were based on the 210 fit of deterministic model projections to each day's case count, under the assumption that these 211 case counts represented independent, Poisson-distributed variables, scaled by the reporting 212 fraction (ρ).

Since the EYE strategy was first implemented in 2017, there has been progress towards eliminating YF epidemics.
However, recent YF events, including an epidemic in the Colombian Andes, highlight persisting gaps in immunization coverage in areas previously thought to be low risk [27].

text.text: While previous studies have evaluated the effects of YF vaccination coverage and delays separately, here we provide a framework to quantify the impact of both factors on YF outbreaks.
We found that the recent outbreaks in Ghana (2021-2022) and South Sudan (2023-2024) are useful archetypes for modeling the effects of YF immunization.
Ghana had a timely local YF vaccination campaign and regional vaccination coverage near the EYE threshold of 80%.

Meanwhile, South Sudan had lower vaccination coverage, longer delays to reactive vaccination, and likely lower detection/reporting of cases -and an observed outbreak size approximately 2.5 times as large.
In both scenarios, our models estimate that increasing baseline immunization coverage and decreasing the time to reactive vaccination would have averted a substantial number of cases and deaths.

Furthermore, our models suggest that baseline vaccination coverage and reactive vaccination timing act non-linearly to influence outbreak size -at any given level of baseline coverage, reducing the time to reactive vaccination averts additional morbidity, and vice versa.
When considering the critical vaccination threshold, we found that the recommended threshold of 80% was effective at mitigating large-scale outbreaks.
However, reaching the 80% threshold (or the 60-80% security range) did not prevent expansion in all circumstances, especially if reactive vaccination was delayed.

This finding aligns with a recent study showing that 80% coverage was effective at reducing the probability of YF outbreaks, yet risk remained in regions with transmission variability and vaccination coverage uncertainty [28].

text.text: Likewise, our findings align with a modeling study of the 2016 YF epidemic in Angola which similarly found that delayed vaccination by 60 days would have increased cases and deaths roughly 3-fold [10].

text.text: These findings have important implications for future YF vaccination strategies.
Both increasing immunization coverage and decreasing the time to reactive vaccination are essential to mitigating outbreaks.
In an ideal scenario, both strategies should be emphasized.
However, in the setting of resource constraints, it is important to consider how countries may prioritize resources.
Our findings demonstrate that baseline YF immunity influences how much response timing matters.
Therefore, a tailored approach to vaccination coverage and response timing may improve resource allocation.

There are limitations to this analysis.
To make the models more generalizable and capture the acute phase of outbreaks, we modeled the human population as closed and the mosquito population as being at equilibrium.
Likewise, we assumed homogeneous mixing and used estimated vaccination coverages, which may affect total trajectory estimates.

For instance, because the Ghana outbreak scenario had high estimated vaccination coverage (70%) and a fast response, sustaining transmission required a greater force of infection, which may overestimate outbreak size in scenarios with lower coverage and longer delays.
We also assumed lifelong immunity from prior YF vaccination.
Despite these limitations, our approach offers a framework for evaluating the synergies and tradeoffs between YF vaccination coverage and response timing.
Overall, the EYE strategy has made significant progress.
Both investment in increased 340 vaccination coverage and timely response have averted YF cases and deaths.
However, YF 341 outbreaks continue to occur, including in areas previously deemed as low risk.
Identifying gaps 342 in vaccination coverage, as well as delays in diagnosis and response, will be key to targeted 343 prevention strategies.
Modeling frameworks such as this can help decision-makers evaluate the 344 relative benefits of these strategies as we enter the next phase towards eliminating YF epidemics.
